slides.say: This is about two travelers at once. How fast do they get closer, or farther apart?
Relative speed is the rate at which the gap between two travelers changes.

slides: We don't follow each one on its own. We follow the gap between them. How many kilometers does the gap change in one hour?

slides.say: Now a new example. Two walkers start twenty-four kilometers apart, and walk toward each other. One walks at three kilometers per hour, and the other at five.

slides: In one hour, the first walker covers three kilometers, and the second covers five. Both of them make the gap smaller.

slides.say: So the gap shrinks by three plus five, eight kilometers every hour.
Picture a head-on crash. The two cars hit with both speeds together. That's why we add the speeds.
The gap is twenty-four kilometers, and it shrinks by eight every hour. Twenty-four divided by eight is three. So they meet after three hours.
Now the same two walkers start from the same point, and walk in opposite directions, away from each other.
In one hour, one walks three kilometers one way, and the other walks five kilometers the other way.
So the gap grows by three plus five, eight kilometers every hour. Opposite directions, so again we add.
at: So the gap grows by three plus five

slides.say: Now a chase. A runner runs at six kilometers per hour. A cyclist rides behind her, on the same road, at nine.
In one hour, the runner moves six kilometers ahead, and the cyclist moves nine. The runner keeps running away, while the cyclist tries to catch up.
So the cyclist gains only nine minus six, three kilometers every hour. In a chase, we subtract.
Say the cyclist starts two kilometers behind her. He closes two kilometers at three kilometers an hour.
Two divided by three is two thirds of an hour. Two thirds of sixty minutes is forty minutes.
So toward each other or apart, we add. In a chase, we subtract. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next part.
